catalog_quote: シベ方言では、高いピッチから始まる強勢音節は原則として最後の音節である。(11) (a) yila [jɪˈlaː]「止まれ」 (b) doχuluN [dɔʁʊˈlun]「びっこ」 ただし、複数音節の語の語末が高母音音素（i, e, u）である場合、語末音節が強勢を受ける語と受けない語がある。強勢を受ける場合はその高母音が音声的に消えず、強勢がその音節に来る（例えば、次の 12(a)）。一方、強勢を受けない場合はその高母音が消えて、強勢がその前の音節に来る（例えば、次の 12(b)）。この場合、アキュート・アクセントを用いて強勢がその音節に来ることを示す。(12) (a) dexamé [dɜɣaˈmɜː]「母の姉妹の夫」 (b) jirame [d͡ʑiˈɾam]「厚い」 高母音音素で終わる 2 音節語は、強勢音節の位置によって意味が異なる場合がある。このような場合、強勢音節の位置によるミニマルペアと見なせる。... (13) (a) muku [mukʷʰ]「羊の踝の骨で作った骰子の 1 つの面の名前」 (b) mukú [muˈkʰuː]「水」 (14) (a) cixe [t͡ɕʰix]「湿気」 (b) cixé [t͡ɕʰiˈɣɜː]「蚤」 ... (17) (a) erde [ɨɾt]「早い」 (b) erdé [ɨɾˈdɜː]「朝」 ... 上記の場合を除いても、稀に例外がある。例えば、次の語は強勢が 1 音節目にある。... (20) guxuN [ˈɡuːɣun]「明るい」 ... [fn. 7] 久保ほか（2011: 10）も語末の i, e, u に限って強勢があるかないかの区別があると記述している。 [fn. 8] 該当する高母音が音声的に消えるが、音韻的にはその母音が存在する。 ... [2] 強勢の位置が弁別的な機能を果たせるか否か 第 3 節で述べたように、三家子方言とシベ方言では強勢の位置が弁別的な機能を果たす場合があるが、黒河方言では強勢の位置が弁別的な機能を果たさない。 ... The position of the stress of the first type may be different in different dialects, and it can distinguish words in Sanjiazi and Sibe.

new_statements.quote: シベ方言では、高いピッチから始まる強勢音節は原則として最後の音節である。(11) (a) yila [jɪˈlaː]「止まれ」 (b) doχuluN [dɔʁʊˈlun]「びっこ」 ただし、複数音節の語の語末が高母音音素（i, e, u）である場合、語末音節が強勢を受ける語と受けない語がある。強勢を受ける場合はその高母音が音声的に消えず、強勢がその音節に来る（例えば、次の 12(a)）。一方、強勢を受けない場合はその高母音が消えて、強勢がその前の音節に来る（例えば、次の 12(b)）。(12) (a) dexamé [dɜɣaˈmɜː]「母の姉妹の夫」 (b) jirame [d͡ʑiˈɾam]「厚い」 高母音音素で終わる 2 音節語は、強勢音節の位置によって意味が異なる場合がある。このような場合、強勢音節の位置によるミニマルペアと見なせる。
new_statements.translation: In the Sibe dialect, the stressed syllable that begins with high pitch is, as a rule, the final syllable. (11) (a) yila [jɪˈlaː] 'stop!' (b) doχuluN [dɔʁʊˈlun] 'lame'. However, when a polysyllabic word ends in a high-vowel phoneme (i, e, u), there are words whose final syllable receives stress and words whose final syllable does not. When it receives stress, that high vowel is not phonetically deleted and the stress falls on that syllable (e.g. 12a). When it does not receive stress, the high vowel is deleted and the stress falls on the preceding syllable (e.g. 12b). (12) (a) dexamé [dɜɣaˈmɜː] 'mother's sister's husband' (b) jirame [d͡ʑiˈɾam] 'thick'. Disyllabic words ending in a high-vowel phoneme can differ in meaning according to the position of the stressed syllable; such cases can be regarded as minimal pairs by stress position.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sibe has a stress accent whose stressed syllable normally begins with high pitch (F or H); in Sibe that syllable is by default the last syllable of the word. The one systematic exception class is words whose underlying final vowel is high (i, e, u): lexically, some keep the vowel and stress it (mukú [muˈkʰuː] 'water', cixé 'flea', erdé 'morning'), others delete it and stress the syllable before it (muku [mukʷʰ] 'dice face', cixe 'damp', erde 'early') — so on the surface stress is still on the phonetically last syllable, but phonemically stress position is contrastive (§5: 'in the Sanjiazi and Sibe dialects the position of stress can serve a distinctive function'). Stress shift can also produce stressed syllables that begin with low pitch (e.g. ale-mi [a˩.ˈlɨm˥] ~ [ˈaː˩.lɨm˧]); the resulting pitch-only near-minimal pairs (tyawe-mi vs tya-mi) are judged not to be tone (§6).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary-stress rule stated. Fn. 10: in a Chapchal compound like coqu yixe 'chicken and duck' each member carries its own stress on its first syllable; the dissertation (2018, §4.1.4) treats the number of stresses as the criterion distinguishing compound (one word) from phrase (two words).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Underlying final high vowels: lexically final-stressed vs. deleted with stress on the preceding syllable (minimal pairs (13)-(17), some from Kubo et al. 2011: 15, 19). (2) Sub-dialects differ: Chapchal yixé [jɪˈɣɜː] 'duck' vs Ichagashan yixe [jɪx]. (3) Verb stem + perfect -xe + modality clitic =i (ji-xe=i 'came') usually stresses the phonetically second-from-last syllable ([ˈd͡ʑiːɣɨj]) rather than the final one; likewise -xaqu=i, -ma=i. (4) Stress shift by sonority difference or syllable consonantization yields low-pitch-onset stressed syllables (jaleN [ɖ͡ʐa˩.ˈlɨn˥] ~ [ˈɖ͡ʐaː˩.lɨn˧]). Other sources disagree: Norman 1974 'penultimate vowel or diphthong' (in a transcription that retains deleted final vowels); Zikmundová 2013 'last syllable of a prosodic unit is usually stressed'; Zikmundová 2023 (snippet) 'main stress normally falling on the first syllable', 'non-distinctive'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: isolated words and inflected word forms (stem + suffix, stem + suffix + clitic) elicited by the author in fieldwork in Chabchal Sibe Autonomous County and Ichagashan township (Huocheng), Xinjiang; phonetic transcriptions with pitch letters. 'Final syllable' means the phonetically final syllable after deletion of unstressed final high vowels. Author treats Sibe as a dialect of Manchu (満洲語シベ方言).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes 満洲語シベ方言, the Sibe spoken in Chabchal (察布査爾) Sibe Autonomous County and Ichagashan (伊車嘎善) township of Huocheng county, Ili, Xinjiang = xibe1242; the author treats it as a dialect of Manchu and contrasts it with Sanjiazi and Heihe Manchu (manc1252). Sub-dialect differences (Chapchal vs Ichagashan) in stress on final high vowels are noted. Hattori & Yamamoto 1956 describe an older Huiyuan speaker (6th/8th banner dialects) of the same language.

sources.note: Manchu has stress accent (強さアクセント); in the Sibe dialect the high-pitch-onset stressed syllable is in principle the final syllable (§3.3 p.155); polysyllables with final high vowel i/e/u split lexically into final-stressed (vowel kept) vs. stress on the preceding syllable (final vowel deleted), giving minimal pairs muku/mukú 'dice face'/'water', cixe/cixé 'damp'/'flea', erde/erdé 'early'/'morning' (p.156); perfect -xe=i forms usually stress the phonetic penult; sub-dialect (Chapchal vs Ichagashan) differences; stress position is distinctive in Sibe (§5 p.163); pitch-like contrasts from stress…

sources.note: Summary and review say ch. 4 (§4.1 pp. 89-96) treats stress: stressed syllables classified into high-pitch and low-pitch stress, then stress position, then number of stresses in compounds vs. phrases; ch. 6 explains low-pitch stress as the result of stress shift (sonority difference, syllable consonantization). The summary itself does not reproduce the Sibe placement rule; bibliography lists 木村滋雄 2002 シベ語のピッチアクセントについて.
